steps.body: Residuals can steer a line as well as diagnose it. Move the line and every residual changes. The least-squares line makes the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible; when the model includes an intercept, its signed residuals also balance to zero.
Steer the line by its leftovers.

widget.prompt: Fit the line so the misses are small and balanced: data (1,3), (2,6), (3,7), (4,9).
widget.successFeedback: At ŷ = 1.9x + 1.5, the residuals are −0.4, +0.7, −0.2, and −0.1. They sum to 0, and their squared sum, 0.70, is the smallest possible.
widget.slopeFeedback: Watch the ENDS: if the first points sit above your line and the last below (or the reverse), the tilt is wrong before the height is.
widget.offsetFeedback: Slope looks right — now the whole cloud sits off to one side. Slide b until the misses straddle the line.

predict.prompt: When the line is fit as well as possible, its leftovers will be…

options.label: Small and balanced — some +, some −, near-zero total
All slightly positive — lines aim under to be safe

predict.reveal: Four points need not lie on one line. The least-squares line balances positive and negative residuals while minimizing their squared total. All-zero residuals are possible when real or simulated data lie exactly on a line.

explanationVariants: Under ŷ = 1.9x + 1.5, the predictions are 3.4, 5.3, 7.2, and 9.1. The residuals are −0.4, +0.7, −0.2, and −0.1, which sum to 0.
A zero signed sum checks that the residuals balance around a fitted line with an intercept. Least squares chooses among such lines by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.

widget.prompt: Under ŷ = 1.9x + 1.5, the residuals are −0.4, +0.7, −0.2, and −0.1. What is their sum?

commonErrors.feedback: 0.70 is the sum of the squared residuals. This question asks for the signed sum: −0.4 + 0.7 − 0.2 − 0.1 = 0.
Keep the signs. The positive 0.7 is balanced by −0.4, −0.2, and −0.1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the four residuals with their signs.
widget.successFeedback: The signed residuals sum to 0. That balance is expected for a least-squares line with an intercept.

explanationVariants: Raising b by 0.7 makes the line hit (2, 6), but it also raises every other prediction by 0.7.
The squared residual total rises from 0.70 to 2.66, so one exact hit makes the overall fit worse.

widget.prompt: Raise the fitted line by 0.7 so it hits (2, 6). What happens to the sum of squared residuals?

options.label: Reject: squared residual total gets larger
options.feedback: The squared total rises from 0.70 to 2.66, so the shifted line fits the four points worse overall.

options.label: Accept: one exact hit makes the fit better
options.feedback: One exact hit is not the goal. Least squares compares the squared residual total across all points.

options.label: Use the signed residual sum to decide
options.feedback: A signed sum can hide large positive and negative misses. Least squares uses the sum of their squares.

widget.successFeedback: Least squares judges the whole set: helping one point does not help if the squared residual total increases.

steps.body: This is the idea behind the 'line of best fit' your tools compute: they choose the slope and intercept that make the residuals collectively smallest (squaring them so ups and downs can't cancel). You've been doing by eye what least squares does by algebra.

hints: Must the best line touch any data point at all?
Consider four points at the corners of a tall X pattern — a line through ANY one of them tilts away from the middle.
The best line balances misses; touching a point is neither required nor rewarded.
explanationVariants: The optimal line can pass between every point — what's minimized is total miss, and touching a point buys nothing.
Best fit is a property of the whole cloud, not of any member: the line often threads empty space.

widget.prompt: Can the best-fit line pass through NONE of the data points?

options.label: Yes: fit quality does not require contact
options.feedback: The line minimizes collective leftovers and often threads between all of them.

options.label: No: it must touch at least one point
options.feedback: Nothing rewards contact. A line through empty space can leave smaller total misses than any point-touching line.

options.label: No: it must touch at least two points
options.feedback: Two-point lines are how you DRAW a line, not how you FIT one.

widget.successFeedback: Fitting serves the cloud, not the individuals — the best line frequently touches nobody.

explanationVariants: Least squares picks m and b minimizing the sum of squared residuals — squaring stops + and − misses cancelling.
Your eyeball procedure and the formula answer the same question: which line leaves the least leftover?

widget.prompt: Software reports 'least-squares line'. Least WHAT, exactly?

options.label: The sum of squared residuals
options.feedback: Squares punish big misses hardest and stop signs from cancelling — then the sum is driven as low as possible.

options.label: The number of points missed
options.feedback: Every line 'misses' nearly all points; counting them can't rank lines.

options.label: The slope
options.feedback: Nothing minimizes slope — a flat line is not automatically a good line.

widget.successFeedback: You fit by residual all lesson; least squares just makes the judgment arithmetic.

takeaways: Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals across all points.
With an intercept, the fitted line's signed residuals sum to zero, but that balance alone does not identify the best line.
An exact hit at one point can still make the overall fit worse.
steps.teaser: Course close: you can now fit a line, use it, and — new — audit it. The residual is the difference between drawing a trend and defending one.
